1.note: Qoheleth is using the possessive form to describe **Flies** that are characterized by **death**. This could mean: (1) flies that have died Alternate translation: [Dead flies] or (2) flies that bring death or disease. Alternate translation: [Flies that bring death] If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way.

The point of this comparison is that just as **Flies of death** can spoil a whole container of **a perfumer’s oil**, so **a little foolishness** can spoil the good that **wisdom** and **honor** have accomplished. Qoheleth implies this comparison by placing the two statements next to each other. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [in the same way, a little foolishness can spoil the good that wisdom or honor has accomplished]

2.note: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a person’s mind and will were his **heart**. It means that what a person thinks and desires guides the way he lives. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The mind of … but the mind of]

Qoheleth is not referring to a specific **wise person** or a specific **fool**. He means wise people and foolish people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [whoever is wise … whoever is foolish]

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the heart could turn **to his right** or **to his left**. In this culture, the right side represented strength and favor, and the left side represented weakness or misfortune. This could mean: (1) a wise person’s understanding protects him, while a fool is exposed to harm. Alternate translation: [it can protect him … it leaves him defenceless] (2) a wise person is inclined toward what is good, while a fool is inclined toward what is evil. Alternate translation: [it leads him toward what is good … it leads him toward what is evil]

3.note: Qoheleth is using the expression that **his heart is lacking** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he lacks good sense.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his mind lacks good sense]

Qoheleth is speaking of the fool’s lack of sense as if it were a living thing that could speak to **everyone**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his behavior shows everyone that he]

4.note: Qoheleth is using **the spirit of the ruler rises against you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the ruler becomes angry with you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ruler becomes angry with you]

Qoheleth is using **do not leave your place** as a common expression of the culture to mean “do not abandon your position.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do not resign from your post]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **calmness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [remaining calm]

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if **great sins** were things that could be caused **to leave**. This could mean: (1) staying calm will cause the ruler to overlook great offenses. Alternate translation: [can reduce the king’s anger at the offenses] (2) staying calm will keep you from committing great sins, such as rebelling against the ruler. Alternate translation: [can keep great offenses from having their effect]

5.note: See how you translated **under the sun** in 1:3.

The point of this comparison is that just as **an unintentional sin** that a ruler commits causes harm even though he did not intend it, so is the **misfortune** that Qoheleth saw harmful. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [which was harmful like an unintentional sin]

Here, **the face** represents the presence of **the authority**. The expression means that the error comes from the ruler himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the authority himself]

6.note: The expression **Folly is placed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, it is the ruler mentioned in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [The ruler places folly] or [The ruler places foolish people]
Here, **Folly** represents foolish people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The foolish person]

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if important positions were **high places** and unimportant positions were **the lowly place**. It means that foolish people are given positions of honor and authority, while rich people are given positions of little importance. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into many positions of honor, and rich people sit in positions of little importance]

7.q: רָאִ֥יתִי עֲבָדִ֖ים עַל־סוּסִ֑ים וְ⁠שָׂרִ֛ים הֹלְכִ֥ים כַּ⁠עֲבָדִ֖ים עַל־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ
7.note: Verses 6 and 7 mean basically the same thing. Verse 6 states the general idea, and verse 7 gives a specific example. Translate these phrases according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. Alternate translation: [Indeed, I saw the social order reversed, with slaves holding high positions and princes brought low]

The implication is that only important and wealthy people rode **horses**, while slaves walked. Qoheleth is saying that the normal order of society has been reversed. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [slaves riding on horses as if they were important and wealthy people]

8.q: חֹפֵ֥ר גּוּמָּ֖ץ & יִפּ֑וֹל בּ֣⁠וֹ & וּ⁠פֹרֵ֥ץ גָּדֵ֖ר & נָחָֽשׁ יִשְּׁכֶ֥⁠נּוּ
8.note: Here Qoheleth uses a proverb in order to warn that people who do risky actions often suffer the consequences of those actions. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Alternate translation: [Whoever digs a hole may fall into it, and whoever tears down a wall may be bitten by a snake]

The implication is that snakes often lived in the cracks of stone walls, so a person who **breaks through a wall** could be bitten by a snake hiding in it. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a snake hiding in the cracks of that wall will bite him]

9.q: מַסִּ֣יעַ אֲבָנִ֔ים יֵעָצֵ֖ב בָּ⁠הֶ֑ם בּוֹקֵ֥עַ עֵצִ֖ים יִסָּ֥כֶן בָּֽ⁠ם
9.note: Here Qoheleth uses or invents a proverb in order to teach that every kind of work carries its own risks, so a wise person takes care while doing it. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. This verse emphasizes the meaning of verse 8 by repeating the same idea using different words. Alternate translation: [Whoever moves stones may be injured by them; whoever chops logs may be harmed by them]

9.q: מַסִּ֣יעַ אֲבָנִ֔ים יֵעָצֵ֖ב בָּ⁠הֶ֑ם בּוֹקֵ֥עַ עֵצִ֖ים יִסָּ֥כֶן בָּֽ⁠ם
9.note: Verses 8 and 9 mean basically the same thing. Verse 9 emphasizes the meaning of verse 8 by repeating the same idea using different words. Translate these phrases according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. Alternate translation: [Indeed, one who pulls up stones or splits wood will be hurt by them]

The expression **will be hurt** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. The word **them** refers to the stones. Alternate translation: [will find that they hurt him]

The expression **will be endangered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. The word **them** refers to the split pieces of wood. Alternate translation: [will find that the pieces endanger him]

10.note: Qoheleth is using **lighten the faces** as a common expression of the culture to mean “sharpen the cutting edge.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. The pronoun **he** refers to the person who is using the axe to cut wood. Alternate translation: [but the person using the axe does not sharpen its cutting edge]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **profit**, **succeeding**, and **wisdom**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [But if a person acts wisely, it will help him to succeed]

11.note: The implication is that the snake bites someone before the snake charmer has used **a charm** to calm it. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [before the snake charmer has used a charm to calm it]

Qoheleth is using **the master of the tongue** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the one who charms snakes with his words.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for the snake charmer]

12.q: דִּבְרֵ֥י פִי חָכָ֖ם חֵ֑ן וְ⁠שִׂפְת֥וֹת כְּסִ֖יל תְּבַלְּעֶֽ⁠נּוּ
12.note: Here Qoheleth uses a proverb in order to teach that wise people speak in ways that bring them goodwill, while fools destroy themselves by what they say. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Alternate translation: [What a wise person says brings him goodwill, but what a fool says will destroy him]

If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **favor**, you could express the same idea in another way. This could mean: (1) the words of a wise person are gracious and pleasing. Alternate translation: [are gracious and pleasing] or (2) the words of a wise person win him the goodwill of others. Alternate translation: [brings him goodwill]

13.q: תְּחִלַּ֥ת דִּבְרֵי פִ֖י⁠הוּ סִכְל֑וּת וְ⁠אַחֲרִ֣ית פִּ֔י⁠הוּ הוֹלֵל֖וּת רָעָֽה
13.note: Qoheleth is referring to the whole of a fool’s speech by naming two extremes, **The beginning of the words of his mouth** and **the end of his mouth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [At first the words of his mouth are foolishness, and in the end what he says is evil insanity]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **insanity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is wickedly insane]

14.note: Qoheleth is not referring to a specific person when he says **Humanity** and **him**. He means people in general, not the fool mentioned earlier in the verse. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [A person]

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and does not know what will happen after he is gone]

Qoheleth is using the question form for emphasis. He means that no one can tell a person what will happen after him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [no one at all can declare it]

15.note: The pronoun **him** refers to each one of the **foolish** people mentioned earlier in the verse. Qoheleth changes from the plural to the singular here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [wearies each one of them]

Qoheleth is using the expression **he does not know how to go to a city** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he is so foolish that he cannot even find his way to town.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he is too foolish to find even the most obvious path]

16.note: Qoheleth is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of grief about the trouble that will come to a land with such leaders. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How terrible it will be for you]

Qoheleth is speaking to a **land** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the harm that bad rulers cause to a nation. He is using **land** to mean the people who live in it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the land. Alternate translation: [people of the land]

The implication is that a king who is **a youth** is not able to rule well. This could mean: (1) the king is young and inexperienced, Alternate translation: [is too young and inexperienced to rule well] or (2) the king is a person of low birth, such as a servant, since the word translated **youth** can also mean “servant.” Alternate translation: [is not able to rule well]. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers.

The implication is that **your princes** are feasting **in the morning**, when they should be working to govern the land. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and your princes feast in the morning when they should be governing you]

17.q: אַשְׁרֵ֣י⁠ךְ אֶ֔רֶץ שֶׁ⁠מַּלְכֵּ֖⁠ךְ בֶּן חוֹרִ֑ים וְ⁠שָׂרַ֨יִ⁠ךְ֙ & יֹאכֵ֔לוּ בָּ⁠עֵ֣ת & בִּ⁠גְבוּרָ֖ה וְ⁠לֹ֥א בַ⁠שְּׁתִֽי
17.note: Verses 16 and 17 mean basically the same thing. For emphasis, Qoheleth is saying it first negatively and then positively. If a speaker of your language would not use repetition like this, in your translation you can convey the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [Blessed are you, land, that your king is a son of nobles and that your princes will eat at the proper time only to gain strength]

Qoheleth is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of happiness for a land that has good leaders. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How happy you are]

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a descendant of noble people were their **son**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is from a noble family]

The implication is that the princes eat and drink only at the proper time for meals, not early in the morning as described in the previous verse. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at the proper time for meals]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **might** and **drunkenness**, you could express the same ideas in another way. This could mean that the princes eat: (1) to gain strength, rather than to get drunk, Alternate translation: [to become strong and not to get drunk] or (2) with self-control, rather than in a drunken way. Alternate translation: [with moderation and not over-indulgence]

18.q: בַּ⁠עֲצַלְתַּ֖יִם & הַ⁠מְּקָרֶ֑ה יִמַּ֣ךְ & וּ⁠בְ⁠שִׁפְל֥וּת יָדַ֖יִם & הַ⁠בָּֽיִת יִדְלֹ֥ף
18.note: Here Qoheleth uses or invents a proverb in order to teach that neglecting needed work leads to damage and loss. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Alternate translation: [When people are lazy, the roof timbers give way, and when people’s hands do nothing, the house lets in rain]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **laziness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [When people are lazy]

Qoheleth is using **hands** to represent the people who should be working with them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and when people are idle]

19.note: Qoheleth is using **bread** to represent food in general, especially the food served at a feast. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a feast]
Here, **silver** represents money. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [but money]

Qoheleth is speaking of **silver** as if it were a living thing that could answer people. He means that money can provide everything that people need. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is useful for obtaining everything]

20.note: The pronoun **your** refers to anyone who reads Qoheleth’s words. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in your thought, my reader]

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if **a bird of the heavens** could **carry the voice** of a person to others. It means that what you say in private may be reported to the people you speak about in ways you would not expect. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what you say may be reported as if a bird of the heavens had carried it]

Qoheleth is using **a master of wings** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a bird.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and a winged creature]
